strengths: The core idea — encoding each digit via sinusoidal components with periods 10, 100, ... (i.e., x mod 10^i) and decoding digits in parallel — is simple, elegant, and directly motivated by interpretability findings (Zhou et al., 2024) that LLMs internally use Fourier features for numbers. The fixed design is justified by an ablation on period choices and by a discussion of why mod-10 aligned frequencies work best.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this line of work: beyond synthetic arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, modular addition, classification), the paper includes (a) a from-scratch GPT-2-117M pretraining run on 10B FineWeb tokens showing FoNE yields the lowest validation perplexity among tokenization schemes, (b) continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-1B on 15B tokens showing improved arithmetic without MMLU degradation, (c) scaling experiments over both data and model size with multiple architectures (GPT-2-Large replication, LayerNorm vs RMSNorm), and (d) a 60-digit addition experiment with chunked FoNE.

Baselines are appropriate and current: digit-wise, subword, xVal, plus an additional appendix comparison with Number Token Loss (NTL) and a combination with Abacus embeddings. The NTL comparison (Tables 15-16) is particularly convincing, showing order-of-magnitude gaps in data efficiency and accuracy.

The discussion section (Q1-Q4) anticipates obvious reviewer questions (regression losses, why periods are powers of 10, LayerNorm/RMSNorm compatibility with a supporting lemma, integration into pretrained models), which strengthens the paper's soundness. Reproducibility statement, detailed algorithms, and hyperparameters are provided.
Efficiency claims (single token per number, 3x-6x fewer tokens, faster training/inference) are supported with concrete measurements (Table 1, WikiTableQuestions token statistics).
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is minimal: Lemma 3.3/D.1 (recovering x mod T from (cos, sin)) and Lemma D.2 (LayerNorm preserves ratios) are elementary and add little beyond justifying design choices. The paper's strength is empirical, not analytical.

The method requires fixed hyperparameters m and n (max integer/decimal digits) set globally for a dataset/model, and the decoding head predicts exactly m+n digits. This raises generality concerns for open-ended language generation: how does the model decide the number of digits to emit, and how are variable-length/leading-zero numbers handled in real text? The chunking workaround for >15 digits is described but only evaluated on synthetic 60-digit addition. Negative numbers, scientific notation, and word-form numbers are only briefly addressed via a parser.

Most headline results (100% accuracy, 64x data efficiency) are on synthetic tasks where the data distribution is known and simple; the real-world evidence (perplexity gains on FineWeb, moderate arithmetic gains in continual pretraining, unchanged MMLU) is encouraging but does not yet demonstrate clear downstream gains on realistic numerical reasoning benchmarks (e.g., quantitative reasoning, tabular QA accuracy).

The comparison of a 38M from-scratch model against a fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B is somewhat apples-to-oranges and is used prominently in the abstract; the from-scratch pretrained 117M model comparison is the more meaningful one.

Novelty is moderate: multi-scale sinusoidal value encodings are closely related to xVal, DICE, SALSA, and standard Fourier/positional features; the contribution is a well-executed and well-validated instantiation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering multiple arithmetic tasks (addition, subtraction, multiplication, decimal, modular), varying training data sizes and model sizes, plus ablations on periods, digit encodings, and architectural variants

The full-pretraining experiment (GPT-2 117M on 10B FineWeb tokens) and continual pretraining on Llama-3.1-1B are valuable and go beyond toy settings, showing FoNE does not harm language modeling perplexity and yields modest downstream gains
The method is simple, parameter-efficient (2 dims per digit), and the token-efficiency analysis (e.g., WikiTableQuestions token counts) is a nice practical touch
The paper is clearly written with detailed algorithms, reproducibility statement, and honest discussion (e.g., float64 precision limits and chunking)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: circular/Fourier number encodings are well explored (xVal, SALSA, DICE, Fourier position embeddings, Zhou et al. 2024), and the core 'theory' (Lemma 3.3/3.4) is elementary — recovering x mod T from (cos, sin) via atan2 is a textbook fact, so the theoretical contribution is thin

Scope is narrow: nearly all evaluations are synthetic arithmetic with fixed-format expressions; there is no evaluation on standard numeracy benchmarks (e.g., table QA accuracy, GSM-style tasks) where the claimed efficiency benefits would matter

The 'single token per number' design requires fixed digit-length hyperparameters (m, n) per dataset/model, a special [NUM] token, and a numeric-string parser; variable-length numbers and chunked >15-digit numbers complicate the claim of seamless integration, and the simplified adaptation for pretrained LLMs is a weaker variant with only moderate gains (Table 4) and no MMLU improvement

The decoding head assumes each digit occupies fixed hidden-state positions, which reduces flexibility and differs from standard autoregressive number generation; implications for general-purpose generation (mixed text/number sequences, formatting like '3.14e-2') are underexplored

Baseline fairness concerns: the 38M scratch-trained model is compared against a fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B, which conflates embedding design with tokenizer/architecture effects; no CoT/scratchpad baseline for the LLM is reported in the main results despite being acknowledged as effective

Claims such as 'only method achieving 100% accuracy' are on narrow self-constructed test sets, and the significance of perfect accuracy on curated synthetic ranges is overstated relative to what practical numeracy requires

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, important problem: numerical representation in LLMs, and grounds the design choice (Fourier features) in interpretability findings (Zhou et al. 2024; Nanda et al. 2023), giving the method a principled rather than ad-hoc justification.

The method is simple, compact (2 dims per digit), and well-specified: embedding, loss, decoding, and integration into a standard tokenizer pipeline are all clearly defined, with algorithms provided in the appendix.

Evaluation is unusually broad for this area: (1) multiple synthetic arithmetic tasks with data-size and model-size sweeps against digit-wise, subword, xVal, and fine-tuned Llama baselines; (2) ablations on period choice, linear-vs-zero-padding, and sinusoidal-vs-direct encoding; (3) combination with Abacus embeddings; (4) 60-digit addition with chunked FoNE; (5) comparison with the recent NTL loss; and importantly (6) language-modeling relevance via GPT-2 pretraining on 10B FineWeb tokens and continual pretraining of Llama-3.1-1B, showing perplexity and arithmetic gains without harming MMLU.

The LayerNorm/RMSNorm invariance analysis (Lemma D.2) is a nice touch that explains why FoNE is more robust than magnitude-based encodings such as xVal, and the ablation on direct digit encoding (Table 14) supports the necessity of sinusoidal structure rather than merely asserting it.
Practical efficiency claims (fewer tokens, faster training/inference, e.g., 149 vs. 329 tokens on WikiTableQuestions) are concrete and quantified.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the circular/modular encoding idea is essentially a rediscovery of standard sinusoidal/Fourier feature constructions (Tancik et al. 2020; Vaswani et al. 2017) applied to number tokens, and the formal lemmas (recovering x mod T via atan2; LayerNorm preserving scaling) are elementary. The paper's strength is empirical packaging more than conceptual depth.

The fixed (m, n) hyperparameterization and the [NUM]-replacement scheme raise real deployment questions that are not fully addressed: handling of out-of-range numbers, mixed formats, negative numbers in free text, and the effect of removing number tokens from the vocabulary on real generation behavior. The fine-tuning/continual-pretraining experiments use a simplified variant, so the headline method's integration into a full-scale LLM remains unverified.

Downstream evaluation beyond synthetic arithmetic is thin. No experiments on realistic numeracy tasks (GSM8K, math word problems, table QA accuracy, time-series forecasting) where the claimed benefits would matter; the MMLU delta (38.10→38.21) is within noise, so the claim that FoNE preserves semantic abilities rests mostly on perplexity.
The FineWeb perplexity improvements (46.8 vs. 48.8 for xVal) are modest, and the paper does not analyze whether they stem from number representation or tokenization-length artifacts.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'the only method that achieves 100% accuracy' holds on tasks curated to be within baseline-competitive ranges (the authors acknowledge this), and a 38M model beating fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B on narrow synthetic arithmetic is not a strong general-capability comparison.

Reproducibility is reasonable on paper (reproducibility statement, hyperparameters, dataset sizes), but no code release is stated, and several results (e.g., Figure 4 heatmaps, production-LLM evaluation in E.1) are hard to verify from the text alone.
